messages.content: Evaluate the Joule coefficient for a van der Waals gas.

solution:
The equation of state is $p = RT / (V - b) - a / V^2$ and so

$$
\left(\frac {\partial p}{\partial T}\right) _ {V} = \frac {R}{V - b}, \tag {27.6}
$$

and hence

$$
\mu_ {\mathrm{J}} = - \frac {1}{C _ {V}} \left[ \frac {R T}{V - b} - \frac {R T}{V - b} + \frac {a}{V ^ {2}} \right] = - \frac {a}{C _ {V} V ^ {2}}. \tag {27.7}
$$

The temperature change in a Joule expansion from $V_{1}$ to $V_{2}$ can be evaluated simply by integrating the Joule coefficient as follows:

$$
\Delta T = \int_ {V _ {1}} ^ {V _ {2}} \mu_ {\mathrm{J}} \mathrm{d} V = - \int_ {V _ {1}} ^ {V _ {2}} \frac {1}{C _ {V}} \left[ T \left(\frac {\partial p}{\partial T}\right) _ {V} - p \right] \mathrm{d} V. \tag {27.8}
$$

messages.content: Evaluate the change in temperature for a van der Waals gas which undergoes a Joule expansion from volume $V_{1}$ to volume $V_{2}$.

solution:
Using eqn 27.8, we have that

$$
\Delta T = - \frac {a}{C _ {V}} \int_ {V _ {1}} ^ {V _ {2}} \frac {\mathrm{d} V}{V ^ {2}} = - \frac {a}{C _ {V}} \left(\frac {1}{V _ {1}} - \frac {1}{V _ {2}}\right) <   0 \tag {27.9}
$$

since $V_{2} > V_{1}$ in an expansion.

messages.content: Assume that the vapour is an ideal gas (so that, for one mole, \(pV_{\mathrm{v}}=RT\)), that the liquid molar volume is negligible compared with the vapour (\(V_{\mathrm{v}}\gg V_{\mathrm{L}}\)), and that the molar heat-capacity difference \(C_{p\mathrm{v}}-C_{p\mathrm{L}}\) is constant. Starting from the Clausius–Clapeyron equation \( \mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}T = L/[T(V_{\mathrm{v}}-V_{\mathrm{L}})] \), evaluate the temperature dependence of the latent heat along the phase boundary in a liquid–gas transition and hence deduce the equation of the phase boundary including this temperature dependence.

solution:
Along the phase boundary, we can write that the gradient in the temperature is (see Fig. 28.5)

$$
\frac {\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} T} = \left(\frac {\partial}{\partial T}\right) _ {p} + \frac {\mathrm{d} p}{\mathrm{d} T} \left(\frac {\partial}{\partial p}\right) _ {T}. \tag {28.24}
$$

Hence, applying this to the quantity $\Delta S = S_{v} - S_{L} = L/T$ where the subscripts v and L refer to vapour and liquid respectively, we have that

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} T} \left(\frac {L}{T}\right) = \left(\frac {\partial (\Delta S)}{\partial T}\right) _ {p} + \frac {\mathrm{d} p}{\mathrm{d} T} \left(\frac {\partial (\Delta S)}{\partial p}\right) _ {T} \\ = \frac {C _ {p v} - C _ {p L}}{T} + \left[ \left(\frac {\partial S _ {v}}{\partial p}\right) _ {T} - \left(\frac {\partial S _ {L}}{\partial p}\right) _ {T} \right] \frac {\mathrm{d} p}{\mathrm{d} T}, (2 8. 2 5) \\ \end{array}
$$

so that

$$
\frac {\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} T} \left(\frac {L}{T}\right) = \frac {C _ {p \mathrm{v}} - C _ {p \mathrm{L}}}{T} - \left[ \frac {\partial}{\partial T} (V _ {\mathrm{v}} - V _ {\mathrm{L}}) \right] \frac {\mathrm{d} p}{\mathrm{d} T}. \tag {28.26}
$$

Using $V_{v} \gg V_{L}$ and $pV_{v} = RT$ , we have that

$$
\frac {\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} T} \left(\frac {L}{T}\right) = \frac {C _ {p \mathrm{v}} - C _ {p \mathrm{L}}}{T} - \frac {R}{p} \times \frac {L p}{R T ^ {2}}, \tag {28.27}
$$

and expanding

$$
\frac {\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} T} \left(\frac {L}{T}\right) = \frac {1}{T} \frac {\mathrm{d} L}{\mathrm{d} T} - \frac {L}{T ^ {2}}, \tag {28.28}
$$

yields

$$
\mathrm{d} L = \left(C _ {p \mathrm{v}} - C _ {p \mathrm{L}}\right) \mathrm{d} T, \tag {28.29}
$$

so that

$$
L = L _ {0} + (C _ {p \mathrm{v}} - C _ {p \mathrm{L}}) T. \tag {28.30}
$$

Thus the latent heat contains a linear temperature dependence and this is shown by the solid line in Fig. 28.4. The slope is negative because $C_{pL} > C_{pv}$ . Substituting this value of L into eqn 28.19 yields the equation of the phase boundary:

$$
p = p _ {0} \exp \left(- \frac {L _ {0}}{R T} + \frac {\left(C _ {p v} - C _ {p L}\right) \ln T}{R}\right). \tag {28.31}
$$

We can also use the Clausius–Clapeyron equation to derive the phase boundary of the liquid–solid coexistence line, as shown in the following example.
answer: \boxed{L = L _ {0} + (C _ {p \mathrm{v}} - C _ {p \mathrm{L}}) T} and \boxed{p = p _ {0} \exp \left(- \frac {L _ {0}}{R T} + \frac {\left(C _ {p v} - C _ {p L}\right) \ln T}{R}\right)}

messages.content: The average temperature in a town in the USA in January is $23^{\circ}$ F and the standard deviation is $9^{\circ}$ F. Convert these figures into degrees Celsius using the relation in Example 3.4.

solution:
The average temperature in degrees Celsius is given by

$$
\langle C \rangle = \frac {5}{9} (\langle F \rangle - 3 2) = \frac {5}{9} (2 3 - 3 2) = - 5 ^ {\circ} \mathrm{C}, \tag {3.31}
$$

and the standard deviation is given by $\frac{5}{9} \times 9 = 5^{\circ}C$ .

messages.content: Suppose that there are n independent random variables, $X_{i}$ , each with the same mean $\langle X\rangle$ and variance $\sigma_{X}^{2}$ . Let Y be the sum of the random variables, so that $Y = X_{1} + X_{2} + \cdots + X_{n}$ . Find the mean and variance of Y.

solution:
The mean of $Y$ is simply

$$
\langle Y \rangle = \left\langle X _ {1} \right\rangle + \left\langle X _ {2} \right\rangle + \dots + \left\langle X _ {n} \right\rangle , \tag {3.34}
$$

but since all the $X_{i}$ have the same mean $\langle X\rangle$ this can be written

$$
\langle Y \rangle = n \langle X \rangle . \tag {3.35}
$$

Hence the mean of $Y$ is $n$ times the mean of the $X_{i}$ . To find the variance of $Y$ , we can use the formula

$$
\sigma_ {Y} ^ {2} = \left\langle Y ^ {2} \right\rangle - \left\langle Y \right\rangle^ {2}. \tag {3.36}
$$

Hence

$$
\langle Y ^ {2} \rangle = \left\langle X _ {1} ^ {2} + \dots + X _ {N} ^ {2} + X _ {1} X _ {2} + X _ {2} X _ {1} + X _ {1} X _ {3} + \dots \right\rangle \tag {3.37}
$$

$$
= \langle X _ {1} ^ {2} \rangle + \dots + \langle X _ {N} ^ {2} \rangle + \langle X _ {1} X _ {2} \rangle + \langle X _ {2} X _ {1} \rangle + \langle X _ {1} X _ {3} \rangle + \dots
$$

There are n terms like $\langle X_{1}^{2}\rangle$ on the right-hand side, and $n(n-1)$ terms like $\langle X_{1}X_{2}\rangle$ . The former terms take the value $\langle X^{2}\rangle$ and the latter terms (because they are the product of two independent random variables) take the value $\langle X\rangle\langle X\rangle=\langle X\rangle^{2}$ . Hence, using eqn 3.35,

$$
\langle Y ^ {2} \rangle = n \langle X ^ {2} \rangle + n (n - 1) \langle X \rangle^ {2}, \tag {3.38}
$$

so that

$$
{\sigma_ {Y} ^ {2}} = {\langle Y ^ {2} \rangle - \langle Y \rangle^ {2}}
$$

$$
= n \langle X ^ {2} \rangle - n \langle X \rangle^ {2}
$$

$$
= n \sigma_ {X} ^ {2}. \tag {3.39}
$$

messages.content: Find the grand potential for a three-dimensional gas of non-interacting bosons and fermions with spin $S$.

solution:
The grand potential $\Phi_{\mathrm{G}}$ is obtained from eqn 30.1 as follows:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \Phi_ {\mathrm{G}} = - k _ {\mathrm{B}} T \ln \mathcal {Z} \\ = \mp k _ {\mathrm{B}} T (2 S + 1) \sum_ {k} \ln (1 \pm \mathrm{e} ^ {- \beta (E _ {k} - \mu)}) \\ = \mp k _ {\mathrm{B}} T \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \ln (1 \pm \mathrm{e} ^ {- \beta (E - \mu)}) g (E) \mathrm{d} E, \tag {30.3} \\ \end{array}
$$

where $g(E)$ is the density of states (containing the spin degeneracy factor $2S+1$ ), which can be derived as follows. States in k-space are uniformly distributed, and so

$$
g (k) \mathrm{d} k = \frac {4 \pi k ^ {2} \mathrm{d} k}{(2 \pi / L) ^ {3}} \times (2 S + 1) = \frac {(2 S + 1) V k ^ {2} \mathrm{d} k}{2 \pi^ {2}}, \tag {30.4}
$$

where $V = L^3$ is the volume. Using $E = {}^2 k^2 / 2m$ we can transform this into

$$
g (E) \mathrm{d} E = \frac {(2 S + 1) V E ^ {1 / 2} \mathrm{d} E}{(2 \pi) ^ {2}} \left(\frac {2 m}{2}\right) ^ {3 / 2}, \tag {30.5}
$$

and hence

$$
\Phi_ {\mathrm{G}} = \mp k _ {\mathrm{B}} T \frac {(2 S + 1) V}{(2 \pi) ^ {2}} \left(\frac {2 m}{2}\right) ^ {3 / 2} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \ln (1 \pm \mathrm{e} ^ {- \beta (E - \mu)}) E ^ {1 / 2} \mathrm{d} E, \tag {30.6}
$$

which after integrating by parts yields

$$
\Phi_ {\mathrm{G}} = - \frac {2}{3} \frac {(2 S + 1) V}{(2 \pi) ^ {2}} \left(\frac {2 m}{2}\right) ^ {3 / 2} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \frac {E ^ {3 / 2} \mathrm{d} E}{\mathrm{e} ^ {\beta (E - \mu)} \pm 1}. \tag {30.7}
$$

The grand potential evaluated in the previous example can be used to derive various thermodynamic functions for fermions and bosons. $^{3}$ Another way to get to the same result is to evaluate the mean occupation $n_{k}$ of a state with wave vector k, which is given by

$$
n _ {\boldsymbol {k}} = k _ {\mathrm{B}} T \frac {\partial}{\partial \mu} \ln \mathcal {Z} _ {\boldsymbol {k}} = \frac {1}{\mathrm{e} ^ {\beta (E _ {\boldsymbol {k}} - \mu)} \pm 1}, \tag {30.8}
$$

and then use this expression to derive directly quantities such as

$$
N = \sum_ {\boldsymbol {k}} n _ {\boldsymbol {k}} = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \frac {g (E) \mathrm{d} E}{\mathrm{e} ^ {\beta (E - \mu)} \pm 1}, \tag {30.9}
$$

and

$$
U = \sum_ {\boldsymbol {k}} n _ {\boldsymbol {k}} E _ {\boldsymbol {k}} = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \frac {E g (E) \mathrm{d} E}{\mathrm{e} ^ {\beta (E - \mu)} \pm 1}. \tag {30.10}
$$

For reasons which will become more clear below, we will write $\mathrm{e}^{\beta \mu}$ as the fugacity $z$ , i.e.,

$$
\boxed {z = \mathrm{e} ^ {\beta \mu}.} \tag {30.11}
$$

These give expressions for $N$ and $U$ as follows:

$$
N = \left[ \frac {(2 S + 1) V}{(2 \pi) ^ {2}} \left(\frac {2 m}{2}\right) ^ {3 / 2} \right] \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \frac {E ^ {1 / 2} \mathrm{d} E}{z ^ {- 1} \mathrm{e} ^ {\beta E} \pm 1} \tag {30.12}
$$

and

$$
U = \left[ \frac {(2 S + 1) V}{(2 \pi) ^ {2}} \left(\frac {2 m}{2}\right) ^ {3 / 2} \right] \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \frac {E ^ {3 / 2} \mathrm{d} E}{z ^ {- 1} \mathrm{e} ^ {\beta E} \pm 1}. \tag {30.13}
$$

$^{3}$ Note that in the derived expressions, the ± sign means + for fermions and - for bosons.

One problem with all these types of formula, such as eqns 30.7, 30.12 and 30.13, is that to simplify them any further, you have to evaluate a difficult integral. Fortunately, we can show that these integrals are related to the polylogarithm function $\operatorname{Li}_n(x)$ (see Appendix C.5), so that

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \frac {E ^ {n - 1} \mathrm{d} E}{z ^ {- 1} \mathrm{e} ^ {\beta E} \pm 1} = (k _ {\mathrm{B}} T) ^ {n} \Gamma (n) [ \mp \mathrm{Li} _ {n} (\mp z) ], \tag {30.14}
$$

where $\Gamma(n)$ is a gamma function. This result is proved in the appendix (eqn C.36). The crucial thing to realize is that $\operatorname{Li}_{n}(z)$ is just a numerical function of z, i.e., of the temperature and the chemical potential. This integral then allows us to establish, after a small amount of algebra, that the number N of particles is given by

$$
N = \frac {(2 S + 1) V}{\lambda_ {\mathrm{th}} ^ {3}} [ \mp \mathrm{Li} _ {3 / 2} (\mp z) ], \tag {30.15}
$$

and the internal energy $U$ is given by

$$
U = \frac {3}{2} k _ {\mathrm{B}} T \frac {(2 S + 1) V}{\lambda_ {\mathrm{th}} ^ {3}} [ \mp \mathrm{Li} _ {5 / 2} (\mp z) ]
$$

$$
= \frac {3}{2} N k _ {\mathrm{B}} T \frac {\mathrm{Li} _ {5 / 2} (\mp z)}{\mathrm{Li} _ {3 / 2} (\mp z)}. \tag {30.16}
$$

We will use these equations in subsequent sections. Note also that we have from eqns 30.7 and 30.13 that

$$
\Phi_ {\mathrm{G}} = - \frac {2}{3} U. \tag {30.17}
$$

messages.content: Evaluate \(N\), \(U\) and \(\Phi_{\mathrm{G}}\) in the ideal-gas limit, using the general results \[ N = \frac{(2S+1)V}{\lambda_{\mathrm{th}}^{3}}[\mp \mathrm{Li}_{3/2}(\mp z)], \qquad U = \frac{3}{2}Nk_{\mathrm{B}}T \frac{\mathrm{Li}_{5/2}(\mp z)}{\mathrm{Li}_{3/2}(\mp z)}, \qquad \Phi_{\mathrm{G}} = -\frac{2}{3}U, \] where \(\beta=1/k_{\mathrm{B}}T\), \(z=e^{\beta\mu}\) is the fugacity, \(\lambda_{\mathrm{th}}=h/\sqrt{2\pi mk_{\mathrm{B}}T}\), and the ideal-gas limit is \(z\ll1\) (equivalently \((N/V)\lambda_{\mathrm{th}}^{3}\ll1\)).

solution:
We choose $z = e^{\beta\mu} \ll 1$ (corresponding to $(N/V)\lambda_{\mathrm{th}}^{3} \ll 1$ ) and use the fact that $\operatorname{Li}_{n}(z) \approx z$ when $z \ll 1$ . Hence elementary substitution yields

$$
N \approx \frac {(2 S + 1) V z}{\lambda_ {\mathrm{th}} ^ {3}}, \tag {30.18}
$$

$$
U \approx \frac {3}{2} N k _ {\mathrm{B}} T, \tag {30.19}
$$

$$
\Phi_ {\mathrm{G}} \approx - N k _ {\mathrm{B}} T. \tag {30.20}
$$

The equation for N shows that the number density of particles N/V is such that, on average, $2S + 1$ particles (one for each spin state) occupy a volume $\lambda_{th}^{3}/z$ . Since $z \ll 1$ , this means that particle wave functions do not overlap. The other two equations are reassuringly familiar. The equation for U asserts that the energy per particle is the well-known equipartition result $\frac{3}{2}k_{B}T$ . The equation for $\Phi_{G}$ , together with $\Phi_{G} = -pV$ (from eqn 22.49) yields the ideal gas law $pV = Nk_{B}T$.

messages.content: Compute the heat capacity of non-interacting free electrons in a three-dimensional metal.

solution:
$$
\begin{array}{l} { U } { = } { \frac { V } { 2 \pi ^ { 2 } } \left( \frac { 2 m } { 2 } \right) ^ { 3 / 2 } \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } E ^ { 3 / 2 } f ( E ) \mathrm{d} E } \\ = \frac {V}{5 \pi^ {2}} \left(\frac {2 m}{2}\right) ^ {3 / 2} \mu (T) ^ {5 / 2} \left[ 1 + \frac {5 \pi^ {2}}{8} \left(\frac {k _ {\mathrm{B}} T}{\mu (0)}\right) ^ {2} + \dots \right] \\ = \frac {3}{5} N \mu (T) \left[ 1 + \frac {\pi^ {2}}{2} \left(\frac {k _ {\mathrm{B}} T}{\mu (0)}\right) ^ {2} + \dots \right] \\ = \frac {3}{5} N \mu (0) \left[ 1 + \frac {5 \pi^ {2}}{1 2} \left(\frac {k _ {\mathrm{B}} T}{\mu (0)}\right) ^ {2} + \dots \right] \tag {30.41} \\ \end{array}
$$

and hence

$$
C _ {V} = \frac {3}{2} N k _ {\mathrm{B}} \left(\frac {\pi^ {2}}{3} \frac {k _ {\mathrm{B}} T}{\mu (0)}\right) + O (T ^ {3}). \tag {30.42}
$$

Thus the contribution to the heat capacity from electrons is linear in temperature (recall from Chapter 24 that the heat capacity from lattice vibrations (phonons) is proportional to $T^{3}$ at low temperature) and will therefore dominate the heat capacity of a metal at very low temperatures.

The Fermi surface is the set of points in k-space whose energy is equal to the chemical potential. If the chemical potential lies in a gap $^{7}$ between energy bands, then the material is a semiconductor or an insulator and there will be no Fermi surface. Thus a metal is a material with a Fermi surface.

messages.content:
Evaluate the following equations for the case $\mu = 0$, where $z = \mathrm{e}^{\beta \mu}$ is the fugacity:
$$
N = \frac{(2S+1)V}{\lambda_{\mathrm{th}}^{3}} \mathrm{Li}_{3/2}(z), \qquad
U = \frac{3}{2} N k_{\mathrm{B}}T \frac{\mathrm{Li}_{5/2}(z)}{\mathrm{Li}_{3/2}(z)}.
$$

solution:
If $\mu = 0$ then $z = 1$ . Now $\operatorname{Li}_n(1) = \zeta(n)$ where $\zeta(n)$ is the Riemann zeta function. Therefore

$$
N = \frac {(2 S + 1) V}{\lambda_ {\mathrm{th}} ^ {3}} \zeta \left(\frac {3}{2}\right) \tag {30.45}
$$

and

$$
U = \frac {3}{2} N k _ {\mathrm{B}} T \frac {\zeta (\frac {5}{2})}{\zeta (\frac {3}{2})}. \tag {30.46}
$$

The numerical values are $\zeta(\frac{3}{2}) = 2.612$ , $\zeta(\frac{5}{2}) = 1.341$ , and hence we have that $\zeta(\frac{5}{2}) / \zeta(\frac{3}{2}) = 0.513$ .

Note that these results will not apply to photons because we have assumed at the beginning that $E = \sqrt[2]{k^{2}/2m}$ , whereas for a photon $E = kc$ . This is worked through in the following example.

messages.content: What is the temperature dependence of the speed of sound assuming adiabatic conditions?

solution:
The relationship between the sound speed $v_{s}$ and the mean square speed of molecules in air $\langle v^{2}\rangle$ given in eqn 31.10 enables us to relate the sound speed in air to its temperature. Using $\langle v^{2}\rangle = 3k_{B}T/m$ , we have that

$$
v _ {\mathrm{s}} = \sqrt {\frac {\gamma \langle v ^ {2} \rangle}{3}} = \sqrt {\frac {\gamma k _ {\mathrm{B}} T}{m}}. \tag {31.11}
$$

This shows that the speed of sound is a function of temperature and mass alone. $^{4}$ It is unsurprising that the speed of sound, i.e., the speed at which a pressure disturbance can be propagated, follows the same temperature dependence as the mean molecular speed since the molecular collision rates that govern the propagation of disturbances are proportional to the mean molecular speed.

messages.content: What is the speed of sound in a relativistic gas?

solution:
For a non-relativistic gas we have from eqn 6.15 that $p = \frac{1}{3}nm \langle v^{2} \rangle$ . Using $\rho = nm$ , we can write this as $p = \frac{1}{3}\rho \langle v^{2} \rangle$ . For a relativistic gas, this should be replaced by

$$
p = \frac {1}{3} \rho c ^ {2}, \tag {31.14}
$$

where $c$ is the speed of light. Since $\rho \propto 1 / V$ , we have that $B = p$ and hence

$$
v _ {\mathrm{s}} = \sqrt {B / \rho} = \frac {c}{\sqrt {3}}. \tag {31.15}
$$

messages.content: Derive an expression for the velocity correlation function $\langle v(0)v(t)\rangle$ for the Brownian motion problem.

solution:
The rate of change of $v$ is given by

$$
\dot {v} (t) = \frac {v (t + \tau) - v (t)}{\tau} \tag {33.17}
$$

in the limit in which $\tau \to 0$ . Inserting this into eqn 33.1 and premultiplying by $v(0)$ gives

$$
\frac {v (0) v (t + \tau) - v (0) v (t)}{\tau} = - \frac {\alpha}{m} v (0) v (t) + \frac {v (0) F (t)}{m}. \tag {33.18}
$$

Averaging this equation, and noting that $\langle v(0)F(t)\rangle = 0$ because v and F are uncorrelated, yields

$$
\frac {\langle v (0) v (t + \tau) \rangle - \langle v (0) v (t) \rangle}{\tau} = - \frac {\alpha}{m} \langle v (0) v (t) \rangle , \tag {33.19}
$$

and taking the limit in which $\tau \rightarrow 0$ yields

$$
\frac {\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} \langle v (0) v (t) \rangle = - \frac {\alpha}{m} \langle v (0) v (t) \rangle , \tag {33.20}
$$

and hence

$$
\langle v (0) v (t) \rangle = \langle v (0) ^ {2} \rangle \mathrm{e} ^ {- \alpha t / m}. \tag {33.21}
$$

This example shows that the velocity correlation function decays to zero as time increases at exactly the same rate that the velocity itself relaxes (see eqn 33.3).

messages.content: A system with a fixed number N of particles is in thermal contact with a reservoir at temperature T. It is surrounded by a tensionless membrane so that its volume is able to fluctuate. Calculate the mean square volume fluctuations. For the special case of an ideal gas, show that $\langle(\Delta V)^{2}\rangle = V^{2}/N$ .

solution:
Fixing $T$ and $N$ means that $U$ can fluctuate. Fixing $N$ implies that $\mathrm{d}N = 0$ and hence we have that

$$
\mathrm{d} U = T \mathrm{d} S - p \mathrm{d} V. \tag {33.50}
$$

Changes in the availability therefore follow:

$$
\mathrm{d} A = \mathrm{d} U - T _ {0} \mathrm{d} S + p _ {0} \mathrm{d} V = (T - T _ {0}) \mathrm{d} S + (p _ {0} - p) \mathrm{d} V, \tag {33.51}
$$

and hence

$$
\left(\frac {\partial A}{\partial V}\right) _ {T, N} = p _ {0} - p \tag {33.52}
$$

and

$$
\left(\frac {\partial^ {2} A}{\partial V ^ {2}}\right) _ {T, N} = - \left(\frac {\partial p}{\partial V}\right) _ {T, N}. \tag {33.53}
$$

Hence

$$
\langle (\Delta V) ^ {2} \rangle = - k _ {\mathrm{B}} T _ {0} \left(\frac {\partial V}{\partial p}\right) _ {T, N}. \tag {33.54}
$$

For an ideal gas, $(\partial V / \partial p)_{T,N} = -Nk_{\mathrm{B}}T / p^{2} = -V / p$ , and hence

$$
\langle (\Delta V) ^ {2} \rangle = \frac {V ^ {2}}{N}. \tag {33.55}
$$

Equation 33.55 implies that the fractional volume fluctuations follow

$$
\frac {\sqrt {\langle (\Delta V) ^ {2} \rangle}}{V} = \frac {1}{N ^ {1 / 2}}. \tag {33.56}
$$

Thus for a box containing $10^{24}$ molecules of gas (a little over a mole of gas), the fractional volume fluctuations are at the level of one part in $10^{12}$ .

We can derive other similar expressions for other fluctuating variables, including

$$
\langle (\Delta T) ^ {2} \rangle = \frac {k _ {\mathrm{B}} T ^ {2}}{C _ {V}}, \tag {33.57}
$$

$$
\langle (\Delta S) ^ {2} \rangle = k _ {\mathrm{B}} C _ {p}, \tag {33.58}
$$

$$
\langle (\Delta p) ^ {2} \rangle = \frac {k _ {\mathrm{B}} T \kappa_ {S}}{C _ {V}}, (3 3. 5 9)
$$

where $\kappa_{S}$ is the adiabatic compressibility (see eqn 16.69).

messages.content: What is the condition for balancing $p_{\mathrm{electron}}$ and $p_{\mathrm{grav}}$ ?

solution:
We set

$$
p _ {\text { electron }} = p _ {\text { grav }}, \tag {36.9}
$$

and using eqns 36.5 and 36.8 this implies that

$$
\rho = \frac {4 G ^ {3} M ^ {2} m _ {\mathrm{e}} ^ {3}}{2 7 \pi^ {3} {} ^ {6}} \left(\frac {A m _ {\mathrm{p}}}{Z}\right) ^ {5}. \tag {36.10}
$$

messages.content: Estimate the minimum rotation period $\tau$ of a pulsar of radius R and mass M.

solution:
For a neutron star rotating at $\omega = 2\pi/\tau$ , the gravitational force at the equator $GM/R^{2}$ must be bigger than the centrifugal force $\omega^{2}R$ , so that

$$
\tau = 2 \pi \sqrt {\frac {R ^ {3}}{G M}}. \tag {36.21}
$$

By analogy with a white dwarf, the mass M of a neutron star follows $M \propto R^{-1/3}$ , so that more massive neutron stars are smaller than lighter ones. When the mass of a neutron star becomes very large, the neutrons behave relativistically and the neutron star becomes unstable.

messages.content:
Many chemical reactions have an activation energy $E_{act}$ of about $\frac{1}{2}$ eV. At T = 300 K, which is about room temperature, the probability that a particular reaction occurs is proportional to

$$
\exp (- E _ {\mathrm{act}} / (k _ {\mathrm{B}} T)). \tag {4.27}
$$

If the temperature is increased to $T + \Delta T = 310 \, \mathrm{K}$ , the probability increases to

$$
\exp (- E _ {\mathrm{act}} / (k _ {\mathrm{B}} (T + \Delta T)), \tag {4.28}
$$

which is larger by a factor

solution:
$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {\exp \left(- E _ {\mathrm{act}} / \left(k _ {\mathrm{B}} (T + \Delta T)\right) \right.}{\exp \left(- E _ {\mathrm{act}} / \left(k _ {\mathrm{B}} T\right)\right)} = \exp \left(- \frac {E _ {\mathrm{act}}}{k _ {\mathrm{B}}} [ (T + \Delta T) ^ {- 1} - T ^ {- 1} ]\right) \\ \approx \exp \left(\frac {E _ {\mathrm{act}}}{k _ {\mathrm{B}} T} \frac {\Delta T}{T}\right) \\ \approx \quad 2. \tag {4.29} \\ \end{array}
$$

Hence many chemical reactions roughly double in speed when the temperature is increased by about 10 K.

messages.content: Calculate the rms speed of a nitrogen $\left(\mathrm{N}_{2}\right)$ molecule at room temperature. [One mole of $N_{2}$ has a mass of 28 g.]

solution: For nitrogen at room temperature, $m = (0.028 \, \text{kg}) / (6.022 \times 10^{23})$ and so $v_{rms} \approx 500 \, m s^{-1}$ . This is about 1100 miles per hour, and is the same order of magnitude as the speed of sound.

messages.content: Air has a density of about $1.29 \, kg m^{-3}$ . Give a rough estimate of the height of the atmosphere assuming that the density of air in the atmosphere is uniform.

solution:
Atmospheric pressure $p \approx 10^{5}$ Pa is due to the weight of air $\rho gh$ in the atmosphere (with assumed height h and uniform density $\rho$ ) pressing down on each square metre. Hence $h = p/\rho g \approx 10^{4}$ m (which is about the cruising altitude of planes). Of course, in reality the density of the atmosphere falls off with increasing height (see Chapter 37).

The pressure p of a volume V of gas (comprising N molecules) depends on its temperature T via an equation of state, which is an expression of the form

$$
p = f (T, V, N), \tag {6.1}
$$

where f is some function. One example of an equation of state is that for an ideal gas, which was given in eqn 1.12:

$$
p V = N k _ {\mathrm{B}} T. \tag {6.2}
$$

Daniel Bernoulli (1700–1782) attempted an explanation of Boyle's law $p \propto 1/V$ by assuming (controversially at the time) that gases were composed of a vast number of tiny particles (see Fig. 6.1). This was the first serious attempt at a kinetic theory of gases of the sort that we will describe in this chapter to derive the ideal gas equation.

messages.content: What is the volume occupied by one mole of ideal gas at standard temperature and pressure (STP, defined as $0^{\circ}$ C and 1 atm)?

solution:
At $p = 1.01325 \times 10^{5}$ Pa and T = 273.15 K, the molar volume $V_{m}$ can be obtained from eqn 6.20 as

$$
V _ {\mathrm{m}} = \frac {R T}{p} = 0. 0 2 2 4 1 4 \mathrm{m} ^ {3} = 2 2. 4 1 4 \text { litres }. \tag {6.22}
$$

messages.content: What is the connection between pressure and kinetic energy density?

solution:
The kinetic energy of a gas molecule moving with speed v is

$$
\frac {1}{2} m v ^ {2}. \tag {6.23}
$$

The total kinetic energy of the molecules of a gas per unit volume, i.e., the kinetic energy density, which we will call u, is therefore given by

$$
u = n \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{2} m v ^ {2} f (v) \mathrm{d} v = \frac {1}{2} n m \langle v ^ {2} \rangle , \tag {6.24}
$$

This expression is true for a non-relativistic gas of particles. For an ultrarelativistic gas, the correct expression is given in eqn 25.21.

so that comparing with eqn 6.15 we have that

$$
p = \frac {2}{3} u. \tag {6.25}
$$

messages.content: Air is 75.5% $N_{2}$ , 23.2% $O_{2}$ , 1.3% Ar, and 0.05% $CO_{2}$ by mass. Calculate the partial pressure of $CO_{2}$ in air at atmospheric pressure.

solution:
Dalton's law states that the partial pressure is proportional to the number density. The number density is proportional to the mass fraction divided by the molar mass. The molar masses of the species (in grammes) are $28(\mathrm{N}_2)$ , $32(\mathrm{O}_2)$ , $40(\mathrm{Ar})$ , and $44(\mathrm{CO}_2)$ . Hence, the partial pressure of $\mathrm{CO}_2$ is

$$
p _ {\mathrm{CO} _ {2}} = \frac {\frac {0 . 0 5}{4 4} \times 1 \mathrm{atm}}{\frac {7 5 . 5}{2 8} + \frac {2 3 . 2}{3 2} + \frac {1 . 3}{4 0} + \frac {0 . 0 5}{4 4}} = 0. 0 0 0 3 3 \mathrm{atm}. \tag {6.28}
$$

# Chapter summary

• The pressure, p, is given by

$$
\boxed {p = \frac {1}{3} n m \langle v ^ {2} \rangle ,}
$$

where n is the number of molecules per unit volume and m is the molecular mass.

\- This expression agrees with the ideal gas equation,

$$
\boxed {p = n k _ {\mathrm{B}} T,}
$$

where V is the volume, T is the temperature and $k_{B}$ is the Boltzmann constant.

messages.content: How much faster does helium gas effuse out of a small hole than $N_{2}$ ?

solution:
$$
\sqrt {\frac {\text { mass   of } \mathrm{N} _ {2}}{\text { mass   of } \mathrm{He}}} = \sqrt {\frac {2 8}{4}} = 2. 6. \tag {7.2}
$$

In this chapter, we will discover where Graham's law comes from. We begin by evaluating the flux of particles hitting the inside walls of the container of a gas.

messages.content: What is the mean kinetic energy of gas molecules effusing out of a small hole?

solution:
$$
\begin{array}{l} \langle \text { kinetic   energy } \rangle = \frac {1}{2} m \langle v ^ {2} \rangle \tag {7.14} \\ { = } { \frac { \frac { 1 } { 2 } m \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } v ^ { 2 } v ^ { 3 } \mathrm{e} ^ { - \frac { 1 } { 2 } m v ^ { 2 } / k _ { \mathrm{B} } T } \mathrm{d} v } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } v ^ { 3 } \mathrm{e} ^ { - \frac { 1 } { 2 } m v ^ { 2 } / k _ { \mathrm{B} } T } \mathrm{d} v } } \\ { = } { \frac { 1 } { 2 } m \left( \frac { 2 k _ { \mathrm{B} } T } { m } \right) \frac { \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } u ^ { 2 } \mathrm{e} ^ { - u } \mathrm{d} u } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } u \mathrm{e} ^ { - u } \mathrm{d} u } } \\ \end{array}
$$

where the substitution $u = mv^{2}/2k_{B}T$ has been made. Using the standard integral $\int_{0}^{\infty} x^{n} e^{-x} dx = n!$ (see Appendix C.1), we have that

$$
\langle \text { kinetic   energy } \rangle = 2 k _ {\mathrm{B}} T. \tag {7.15}
$$

This is larger by a factor of $\frac{4}{3}$ than the mean kinetic energy of molecules in the gas. This is because effusion preferentially selects higher energy molecules.

The hole has to be small. How small? The diameter of the hole has to be much less $^{2}$ than the mean free path $\lambda$ , defined in Section 8.3.

messages.content: Calculate the mean free path for a gas of $N_{2}$ at room temperature and pressure. (For $N_{2}$ , take the molecular diameter to be d = 0.37 nm.)

solution:
The collision cross-section is $\pi d^{2}=4.3\times10^{-19}~m^{2}$ . We have $p\approx10^{5}~Pa$ and $T\approx300~K$ , so the number density is $n=p/k_{\mathrm{B}}T\approx10^{5}/(1.38\times10^{-23}\times300)\approx2\times10^{25}~m^{-3}$ . This leads to $\lambda=1/(\sqrt{2}n\sigma)=6.8\times10^{-8}~m$ .

$^{4}$ Equation 7.23 implies that $\langle v\rangle/\sqrt{\langle v^{2}\rangle} = \sqrt{\frac{8}{3\pi}} = 0.92, \text{ so the error is less than } 10\%.$

$^{5}$ Although this derivation has used an approximation, it turns out that eqn 8.20 is exact. A brief version of the full derivation is given here. Consider a first class of molecules which move at velocity v and consider only collisions with a second class of molecules which move at velocity u. In a frame moving at velocity u, this second class of molecules are stationary and offer a total cross-section of $n\sigma f(\mathbf{u})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{u}$ , where $f(\mathbf{u}) = g(u_x)g(u_y)g(u_z)$ is a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution for the vector $\mathbf{u} = (u_x, u_y, u_z)$ . In unit time, the total volume swept out by these targets relative to the first class of molecules (which in this frame move at velocity v - u) is $|v - u|n\sigma f(\mathbf{u})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{u}$ . The number of encounters per second is obtained by multiplying this volume by the probability of finding one of the first class of molecules in unit volume, giving $|v - u|n\sigma f(\mathbf{u})\,\mathrm{d}u f(\mathbf{v})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{v}$ . The collision rate R is therefore obtained by integrating over all u and v giving

$$
R = n \sigma \int \int | \boldsymbol {v} - \boldsymbol {u} | f (\boldsymbol {u})   \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {u} f (\boldsymbol {v})   \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {v},
$$

which writing $\pmb{x} = (\pmb{v} - \pmb{u}) / \sqrt{2}$ and $\pmb{y} = (\pmb{v} + \pmb{u}) / \sqrt{2}$ can be transformed into

$$
R = n \sigma \sqrt {2} \int | \boldsymbol {x} | f (\boldsymbol {x}) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {x} \int f (\boldsymbol {y}) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {y},
$$

where the first integral yields $\langle v\rangle$ and the second integral is unity. Hence $R = n\sigma\sqrt{2}\langle v\rangle$ and the mean free path is $\lambda = \langle v\rangle/R = 1/(\sqrt{2}n\sigma)$ .

Notice that both $\lambda$ and $\tau$ decrease with increasing pressure at fixed temperature. Thus the frequency of collisions increases with increasing pressure.

# Chapter summary

\- The mean scattering time is given by

$$
\boxed {\tau = \frac {1}{n \sigma \langle v _ {\mathrm{r}} \rangle},}
$$

where the collision cross-section is $\sigma = \pi d^{2}$ , d is the molecular diameter and $\langle v_{r} \rangle \approx \sqrt{2} \langle v \rangle$ .

\- The mean free path is

$$
\boxed {\lambda = \frac {1}{\sqrt {2} n \sigma}.}
$$

messages.content: What is the mass of 3 moles of carbon dioxide $(\mathrm{CO}_2)$ ? (1 mole of oxygen atoms has a mass of $16\mathrm{g}$ .)

A typical bacterium has a mass of $10^{-12}\mathrm{g}$ . Calculate the mass of a mole of bacteria. (Interestingly, this is about the total number of bacteria living in the guts of all humans resident on planet Earth.) Give your answer in units of elephant-masses (elephants have a mass $\approx 5000\mathrm{kg}$ ).

solution:
$$10^{-12}\text{ g is }10^{-15}\text{ kg}.$$

$$1\text{ mole of bacteria } = 6\times10^{23}\times10^{-15}=6\times10^{8}\text{ kg}$$

$$\text{i.e. }\approx 1.2\times10^{5}\text{ elephant-masses}$$

messages.content:
One face of a thick uniform layer is subject to sinusoidal temperature variations of angular frequency $\omega$ . Show that damped sinusoidal temperature oscillations propagate into the layer and give an expression for the decay length of the oscillation amplitude. A cellar is built underground and is covered by a ceiling, which is $3\mathrm{m}$ thick and made of limestone. The outside temperature is subject to daily fluctuations of amplitude $10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and annual fluctuations of $20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . Estimate the magnitude of the daily and annual temperature variations within the cellar. Assuming that January is the coldest month of the year, when will the cellar's temperature be at its lowest?

[The thermal conductivity of limestone is $1.6 \, Wm^{-1} \, K^{-1}$ , and the heat capacity of limestone is $2.5 \times 10^{6} \, J \, K^{-1} \, m^{-3}$ .]

solution:
A trial solution of $T(x,t) = T(0,0)\mathrm{e}^{i(kx - \omega t)}$ in the one-dimensional thermal diffusion equation

$$
\frac {\partial T}{\partial t} = \frac {\kappa}{C} \frac {\partial^ {2} T}{\partial x ^ {2}}
$$

(where $C$ is a heat capacity per unit volume) yields $-\mathrm{i}\omega = \frac{\kappa}{C} (-k^2)$ . In this problem $\omega$ must be real so we write

$$
k = \pm (1 + \mathrm{i}) \sqrt {\frac {\omega C}{2 \kappa}} = \pm \frac {1 + \mathrm{i}}{\delta}
$$

where $\delta = \sqrt{2\kappa / \omega C}$ is the skin depth. We choose the sign of $k$ to get the right boundary condition: here positive so that it doesn't blow up as $x \to \infty$ . Hence for $x \geq 0$ we can write in general

$$
T (x, t) = \sum_ {\omega} A _ {\omega} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \mathrm{i} \omega t} \mathrm{e} ^ {(\mathrm{i} - 1) x / \delta}.
$$

If the boundary condition at the surface is then $T(0,t) = T_0 + T_1\cos \omega t$ then matching terms we get

$$
T (x, t) = T _ {0} + T _ {1} \cos (\omega t - \frac {x}{\delta}) \mathrm{e} ^ {- x / \delta}.
$$

Putting in the numbers, for daily fluctuations $\delta = 0.13$ m and the fluctuations in the cellar are nanoKelvin! Annual fluctuations give $\delta = 2.5$ m and the fluctuations in the cellar come out to about $6^{\circ}C$ . The phase lag can be estimated from the $\omega t - \frac{x}{\delta}$ term. The minimum will occur at a time $t_{0}$ when $\omega t_{0} = \frac{x}{\delta}$ , so that putting in the numbers I get $t_{0}$ is about 68–70 days, i.e. in March.
answer: \boxed{\delta = \sqrt{\frac{2\kappa}{\omega C}}}, \boxed{T(x,t) = T_0 + T_1 \cos(\omega t - x/\delta) e^{-x/\delta}}, \boxed{\text{Daily: } \sim 10^{-9}\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}}, \boxed{\text{Annual: } \sim 6\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}}, \boxed{\text{Minimum in March}}

messages.content: Show that for a spherical chicken of radius \(a\), initially at uniform temperature \(T_0\), placed in an oven at temperature \(T_1\) at time \(t=0\) (so that its surface is maintained at \(T_1\)), the centre temperature \(T\) gets \(90\%\) of the way from \(T_0\) to \(T_1\) after a time \(\sim a^2 \ln 20 / \pi^2 D\), where \(D\) is the thermal diffusivity.

solution:
We want to find $[T_1 - T(0,t)] / [T_1 - T_0] = 0.1$ , which implies that

$$
2 \mathrm{e} ^ {- D (\pi / a) ^ {2} t} = 0. 1
$$

and hence $D(\pi / a)^2 t = \ln 20$ and the result follows.

messages.content:
For oscillations at frequency $\omega$, a viscous penetration depth $\delta_{\mathrm{v}}$ can be defined by

$$
\delta_{\mathrm{v}} = \left(\frac {2 \eta}{\rho \omega}\right) ^ {1 / 2}, \tag {10.76}
$$

analogously to the thermal penetration depth

$$
\delta = \left(\frac {2 \kappa}{\rho c _ {p} \omega}\right) ^ {1 / 2} \tag {10.77}
$$

Show that

$$
\left(\frac {\delta_{\mathrm{v}}}{\delta}\right) ^ {2} = \sigma_{\mathrm{p}}, \tag {10.78}
$$

where $\sigma_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the Prandtl number, defined as $\sigma_{\mathrm{p}} = \eta c_p/\kappa$.

solution: $(\delta_v / \delta)^2 = \eta c_p / \kappa = \sigma_{\mathrm{p}}$

messages.content: The space between two concentric cylinders is filled with material of thermal conductivity $\kappa$ . The inner (outer) cylinder has radius $r_1(r_2)$ and is maintained at temperature $T_{1}(T_{2})$ . Derive an expression for the heat flow per unit length between the cylinders.

solution:
In cylindrical geometry, we have that

$$
\frac {\partial}{\partial r} \left(r \frac {\partial T}{\partial r}\right) = 0
$$

and hence

$$
r \frac {\partial T}{\partial r} = \text { const }
$$

and so

$$
\frac {\partial T}{\partial r} = \frac {\text { const }}{r}.
$$

Hence

$$
T _ {2} - T _ {1} = \int_ {r _ {1}} ^ {r _ {2}} \frac {\operatorname{const} r}{r} = \operatorname{const} \ln \frac {r _ {2}}{r _ {1}},
$$

which fixes the value of the const. At $r = r_1$ , we can write

$$
J = - \kappa \frac {\partial T}{\partial r} = - \kappa \frac {\text { const }}{r _ {1}} = \frac {\kappa (T _ {1} - T _ {2})}{r _ {1} \ln (r _ {2} / r _ {1})}.
$$

Hence the heat flow per unit length, which is $2\pi r_{1}J$ is given by

$$
\frac {2 \pi \kappa (T _ {1} - T _ {2})}{\ln (r _ {2} / r _ {1})}.
$$

messages.content:
One mole of ideal monatomic gas is confined in a cylinder by a piston and is maintained at a constant temperature $T_0$ by thermal contact with a heat reservoir. The gas slowly expands from $V_1$ to $V_2$ while being held at the same temperature $T_0$ . Why does the internal energy of the gas not

change? Calculate the work done by the gas and the heat flow into the gas.

solution:
For an ideal gas, $\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T = 0$ and hence $U$ doesn't change.

$$
\Delta W = \int_{V_1}^{V_2} (-p) \mathrm{d}V = \int_{V_1}^{V_2} -\frac{R T_0 \mathrm{d}V}{V} = -R T_0 \ln(V_2 / V_1).
$$

The work done by the gas is $RT_0 \ln(V_2 / V_1)$.

The heat flow into the gas is $RT_0 \ln(V_2 / V_1)$, since $\Delta U = 0$.
answer: \boxed{\text{Internal energy does not change because } \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T = 0 \text{ for an ideal gas.}} \boxed{W = R T_0 \ln(V_2 / V_1)} \boxed{Q = R T_0 \ln(V_2 / V_1)}

messages.content:
Consider the differential

$$
\mathrm{d} z = 2 x y \mathrm{d} x + (x ^ {2} + 2 y) \mathrm{d} y. \tag {11.39}
$$

Evaluate the integral $\int_{(x_1,y_1)}^{(x_2,y_2)}\mathrm{d}z$ along the paths consisting of straight-line segments

(i) $(x_{1},y_{1})\rightarrow(x_{2},y_{1})$ and then $(x_{2},y_{1})\rightarrow(x_{2},y_{2})$ .
(ii) $(x_{1},y_{1}) \rightarrow (x_{1},y_{2})$ and then $(x_{1},y_{2}) \rightarrow (x_{2},y_{2})$ .

Is $dz$ an exact differential?

solution:
If $f = x^{2}y + y^{2}$ , then $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 2xy$ and $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = x^{2} + 2y$ . It is an exact differential. Both methods of integration lead to

$$
x _ {2} ^ {2} y _ {2} - y _ {1} x _ {1} ^ {2} + y _ {2} ^ {2} - y _ {1} ^ {2}.
$$

messages.content:
In an adiabatic expansion of an ideal gas, $pV^{\gamma}$ is constant. Show also that

$$
T V ^ {\gamma - 1} = \text { constant }, \tag {12.23}
$$

$$
T = \text { constant } \times p ^ {1 - 1 / \gamma}. \tag {12.24}
$$

solution: Start with $pV^{\gamma}$ is constant and then substitute in $pV \propto T$. From $pV \propto T$, we have $p \propto T/V$. Substituting into $pV^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$ gives $(T/V) V^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$, so $T V^{\gamma-1} = \text{constant}$, which is Eq. (12.23). For the second relation, from $pV \propto T$ we have $V \propto T/p$. Substituting into $pV^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$ gives $p (T/p)^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$, so $p^{1-\gamma} T^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$, or $T = \text{constant} \times p^{1-1/\gamma}$, which is Eq. (12.24).

messages.content: Using the relation \(\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial V}\right)_{\text{adiabatic}} = \gamma \left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial V}\right)_T\), relate the gradients of adiabats and isotherms on a \(p - V\) diagram.

solution: The adiabat has a steeper gradient by a factor of $\gamma$.

messages.content: A heat pump has an efficiency greater than 100%. Does this violate the laws of thermodynamics?

solution: No: consider the definition of efficiency for a heat pump.

messages.content: What is the maximum possible efficiency of an engine operating between two thermal reservoirs, one at $100^{\circ}$ C and the other at $0^{\circ}$ C?

Two identical bodies of constant heat capacity $C_{p}$ at temperatures $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$ respectively are used as reservoirs for a heat engine. If the bodies remain at constant pressure, show that the amount of work obtainable is

$$
W = C _ {p} \left(T _ {1} + T _ {2} - 2 T _ {\mathrm{f}}\right), \tag {13.43}
$$

where $T_{f}$ is the final temperature attained by both bodies. Show that if the most efficient engine is used, then $T_{f}^{2} = T_{1}T_{2}$ .

solution:
The energy available from body 1 is $C_p(T_1 - T_f)$ . The energy available from body 2 is $C_p(T_2 - T_f)$ . Hence $W = C_p(T_1 + T_2 - 2T_f)$ .

The most efficient engine is reversible and so using the Clausius theorem, the integral round a closed loop of $\mathrm{d}Q / T$ is zero, and hence $\int_{T_1}^{T_f}C_p\mathrm{d}T / T + \int_{T_2}^{T_f}C_p\mathrm{d}T / T = 0$ and the result follows. (This result can equivalently be derived by stating $\Delta S = 0$ , using the entropy $S$ defined in the following chapter.)

messages.content:
A building is maintained at a temperature $T$ by means of an ideal heat pump, which uses a river at temperature $T_0$ as a source of heat. The heat pump consumes power $W$ , and the building loses heat to its surroundings at a rate $\alpha(T - T_0)$ , where $\alpha$ is a positive constant. Show that $T$ is given by

$$
T = T _ {0} + \frac {W}{2 \alpha} \left(1 + \sqrt {1 + 4 \alpha T _ {0} / W}\right). \tag {13.44}
$$

solution:
In the steady state $\alpha(T-T_{0})$ is balanced by the heat power coming from the heat pump, call it $Q_{2}=W+Q_{1}$ where $Q_{1}$ is the heat power extracted from the river. The efficiency

$$
\eta = \frac {Q _ {2}}{W} = \frac {T}{T - T _ {0}},
$$

so rearranging gives

$$
\alpha (T - T _ {0}) = \frac {T W}{T - T _ {0}}
$$

and hence $TW = \alpha(T - T_{0})^{2}$ which is a quadratic in T. Easiest perhaps to solve for $t = T - T_{0}$ so that $t^{2} - tW/\alpha - T_{0}W/\alpha = 0$ and the result follows (use the positive root of the quadratic or you have a cooling effect and in this country we tend to think of needing to keep our houses warmed not cooled).

messages.content: Three identical bodies of constant thermal capacity are at temperatures 300 K, 300 K, and 100 K. If no work or heat is supplied from outside, what is the highest temperature to which any one of these bodies can be raised by the operation of heat engines? If you set this problem up correctly you may have to solve a cubic equation. This looks hard to solve but in fact you can deduce one of the roots [Hint: what is the highest temperature of the bodies if you do nothing to connect them?].

solution:
To save writing lots of zeros, I will measure temperature in units of $100\mathrm{K}$ . In these units we have temperatures as follows:

initially: 3, 3, 1

finally: $T_{1}, T_{1}, T_{2}$

Energy conservation implies that $2T_{1} + T_{2} = 7$ .

Connecting them with reversible heat engines implies that $2 \ln T_{1} + \ln T_{2} = 2 \ln 3 + \ln 1$ and so $T_{1}^{2}T_{2} = 9$ . Putting this altogether gives a cubic $T_{1}^{3} - \frac{7}{2}T_{1}^{2} + \frac{9}{2} = 0$ .

This could be nasty to solve, except that a solution must be $T_{1}=3$ (when you connect up the reversible engines but run them for zero time!) so therefore you know one root. Hence $(T_{1}-3)(T_{1}^{2}+\alpha T_{1}+\beta)=0$ and equating coefficients you can deduce $\alpha$ and $\beta$ and arrive at $(T_{1}-3)(T_{1}-\frac{3}{2})(T_{1}+1)=0$ so the other positive root is $T_{1}=\frac{3}{2}$ (or 150 K in proper units) and hence $T_{2}=4$ (or 400 K in proper units).

messages.content: A mug of tea has been left to cool from $90^{\circ}$ C to $18^{\circ}$ C. If there is 0.2 kg of tea in the mug, and the tea has specific heat capacity $4200\ J\ K^{-1}\ kg^{-1}$ , show that the entropy of the tea has decreased by $185.7\ J\ K^{-1}$ . Comment on the sign of this result.

solution: $\Delta S = -\int_{291}^{363} \frac{CdT}{T} = -C \ln(363/291) = -185.7 \, J \, K^{-1}$ . It is negative but the entropy in the surroundings changes by $C(363 - 291)/291 = +207.8 \, J \, K^{-1}$ which is positive and larger. Hence the entropy of the Universe goes up.

messages.content: In a typical microchip, a bit is stored by a 5 fF capacitor using a voltage of 3 V. Calculate the energy stored in eV per bit and compare this with the minimum heat dissipation by erasure, which is $k_{B}T \ln 2$ per bit, at room temperature.

solution: $C = 5 \times 10^{-15} \mathrm{~F}$ and $V = 3 \mathrm{~V}$ gives $\frac{1}{2} C V^2 = 1.4 \times 10^5 \mathrm{eV}$ which is much larger than $k_{\mathrm{B}} T \ln 2 \approx 0.02 \mathrm{eV}$.

messages.content:
A particular logic gate takes two binary inputs $A$ and $B$ and has two binary outputs $A'$ and $B'$ . Its truth table is
AB $A'$ $B'$
0011
0110
1001
1100
and the operations producing these outputs are $A' = NOT A$ and $B' = NOT B$ . The input has a Shannon entropy of 2 bits. Show that the output has a Shannon entropy of 2 bits. A second logic gate has a truth table given by
AB $A'$ $B'$
0000
0110
1010
1111
This can be achieved using $A' = A$ OR B and $B' = A$ AND B. Show that the output now has an entropy of $\frac{3}{2}$ bits. What is the crucial difference between the two logic gates?

solution:
(a) $S = -\sum_{i} P_{i} \log_{2} P_{i} = -\frac{1}{4} \log_{2} \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4} \log_{2} \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4} \log_{2} \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4} \log_{2} \frac{1}{4} = \log_{2} 4 = 2$ bits.

(b) $S = -\sum_{i} P_{i} \log_{2} P_{i} = -\frac{1}{4} \log_{2} \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4} \log_{2} \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{2} \log_{2} \frac{1}{2} = \frac{3}{2}$ bits. Information has been lost. The gate is not reversible.
answer: \boxed{2\text{ bits}},\boxed{\frac{3}{2}\text{ bits}},\boxed{\text{The first gate is reversible; the second is not.}}

solution:
Set $k = 1$ and use Lagrange multipliers.

$$
S = - \sum_ {i} P _ {i} \ln P _ {i} - \alpha \sum_ {i} P _ {i} - \beta \sum_ {i} P _ {i} f (x _ {i})
$$

and differentiate with respect to $P_{j}$ , yielding

$$
- \ln P _ {j} - 1 - \alpha - \beta f (x _ {j}) = 0
$$

and hence

$$
P _ {j} = \mathrm{e} ^ {- 1 - \alpha} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \beta f (x _ {j})}.
$$

The first exponential can be got rid off by using the constraint that $\sum P_{i} = 1$ and writing the answer as

$$
P _ {j} = \frac {1}{Z (\beta)} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \beta f (x _ {j})}
$$

with $Z(\beta)$ as defined in the question. The final result follows straightforwardly from

$$
\langle f (x _ {j}) \rangle = \sum_ {j} f (x _ {j}) P _ {j}.
$$

messages.content:
In a TV game show, a contestant is shown three closed doors. Behind one of the doors is a shiny expensive sports car, but behind the other two are goats. The contestant chooses one of the doors at random (she has, after all, a one-in-three chance of winning the car). The game show host (who knows where the car is really located) flings open one of the other two doors to reveal a goat. He grins at the contestant and says: “Well done, you didn’t pick the goat behind this door.” (Audience applauds sycophantically.) He then adds, still grinning: “But do you want to swap and choose the other closed door or stick with your original choice?” What should she do?

This page intentionally left blank

solution:
This is the “Monty Hall problem” and is a deceptively hard question. Many people think that it doesn’t make any difference, but it does. She should swap.

The easiest way of seeing this is to say, for the sake of argument, that the contestant chooses door number one. Then there are three possibilities:

- The car is behind door number one: the host will open door number two or three to reveal a goat. In this case, swapping is the wrong thing to do and will lead to LOSING the car.   
- The car is behind door number two: the host will open door number three to reveal a goat. In this case, swapping is the right thing to do and will lead to WINNING the car.   
- The car is behind door number three: the host will open door number two to reveal a goat. In this case, swapping is the right thing to do and will lead to WINNING the car.

The probability that she picked the right door first time was 1/3. With the additional information given, the probability that the car is behind the other, unopened door, is now 2/3.

[If a student doesn't get this, try the following variant of the problem: you have 100 doors, 99 of which conceal a goat and only one the car. The contestant makes a choice, and the game show host opens 98 of the other doors to reveal a goat behind which. Now the car can either be behind the door the contestant chose or the other non-opened door. It's now pretty obvious that the contestant should switch.]

messages.content:
Consider a liquid of density $\rho$ with molar mass M. Explain why the number of molecules per unit area in the surface is approximately

$$
(\rho N _ {\mathrm{A}} / M) ^ {2 / 3}. \tag {17.47}
$$

Hence, the energy contribution per molecule to the surface tension $\gamma$ is approximately

$$
\gamma / (\rho N _ {\mathrm{A}} / M) ^ {2 / 3}. \tag {17.48}
$$

Evaluate this quantity for water (surface tension at $20\;^{\circ}C$ is approximately $72\;mJ\;m^{-2}$ ) and express your answer in eV. Compare your result with the latent heat per molecule (the molar latent heat of water is $4.4\times10^{4}\;J\;mol^{-1}$ ).

solution: The number of molecules per unit volume is $N_{A}\rho/M$, so at a surface you expect the number per unit area to go as the 2/3 power of this. Putting in the numbers yields 0.043 eV per molecule, which is less than 0.45 eV per molecule which is what the latent heat works out as.

messages.content: What is the mean kinetic energy in eV at room temperature of a gaseous (a) He atom, (b) Xe atom, (c) Ar atom, and (d) Kr atom. [Hint: do you have to make four separate calculations?]

solution: A trick question. The mean kinetic energy is the same for each case, $\frac{3}{2} k_{\mathrm{B}}T = 38\,\mathrm{meV}$.

messages.content:
Comment on the following values of molar heat capacity in $J K^{-1} mol^{-1}$ , all measured at constant pressure at 298 K.
Al24.35Pb26.44
Ar20.79Ne20.79
Au25.42 $N_{2}$ 29.13
Cu24.44 $O_{2}$ 29.36
He20.79Ag25.53
$H_{2}$ 28.82Xe20.79
Fe25.10Zn25.40
[Hint: express them in terms of $R$ ; which of the substances is a solid and which is gaseous?]

solution: $C_{p} = C_{V} + R$ and $C_{p} = \frac{5}{2}R = 20.785$ (for a gas with only translational modes excited or a monatomic gas; i.e. Ar, He, Ne, Xe), $C_{p} = \frac{7}{2}R = 29.099$ (for a gas with translational and rotational modes excited; $H_{2}$ , $N_{2}$ , $O_{2}$ ), and $C_{p} = 3R = 24.94$ (for solids, such as Al, Au, Cu, Fe, Pb, Ag and Zn).
answer: \boxed{C_p = \frac{5}{2}R = 20.785\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}\text{ for Ar, He, Ne, Xe (monatomic gases)}}, \boxed{C_p = \frac{7}{2}R = 29.099\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}\text{ for H_2, N_2, O_2 (diatomic gases)}}, \boxed{C_p = 3R = 24.94\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}\text{ for Al, Au, Cu, Fe, Pb, Ag, Zn (solids)}}

messages.content:
A particle at position $r$ is in a potential well $V(r)$ given by

$$
V (r) = \frac {A}{r ^ {n}} - \frac {B}{r}, \tag {19.28}
$$

where A and B are positive constants and n > 2.

Show that the bottom of the well is approximately quadratic in $r$ . Hence find the particle's mean thermal energy at temperature $T$ above the bottom of the well assuming the validity of the equipartition theorem in this situation.

solution: Taking the well as a one-dimensional problem, $dV / dr = 0$ gives a minimum at $r_0^{n - 1} = nA / B$ and one can Taylor expand around the bottom of this well to show that $V = V_{0} + \alpha (r - r_{0})^{2}$ where $\alpha$ is a constant. The particle can execute simple harmonic motion around the bottom of this well, giving two degrees of freedom (one kinetic, one potential), and so the mean thermal energy is $2\times \frac{1}{2} k_{\mathrm{B}}T = k_{\mathrm{B}}T$.

messages.content: If the energy $E$ of a system is not quadratic, but behaves like $E = \alpha |x|$ where $\alpha > 0$ , show that the average energy is $\langle E \rangle = k_{\mathrm{B}}T$ .

solution:
Writing $E = \alpha |x|$, we have $\mathrm{d}E = \alpha \, \mathrm{d}x$ and $\mathrm{d}x = \alpha^{-1} \, \mathrm{d}E$. Hence

$$
\langle E \rangle = \frac {\int_ {0} ^ {\infty} E \mathrm{e} ^ {- \beta E} \mathrm{d} x}{\int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \beta E} \mathrm{d} x} = \frac {\int_ {0} ^ {\infty} E \mathrm{e} ^ {- \beta E} \mathrm{d} E}{\int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \beta E} \mathrm{d} E} = k _ {\mathrm{B}} T.
$$

messages.content: If the energy $E$ of a system behaves like $E = \alpha |x|^n$ , where $n = 1,2,3\dots$ and $\alpha >0$ , show that the average energy is $\langle E\rangle = \xi k_{\mathrm{B}}T$ , where $\xi$ is a numerical constant.

solution:
Writing $E = \alpha |x|^n$ , we have $\mathrm{d}E = n\alpha |x|^{n - 1}\mathrm{d}x = \frac{nE}{|x|}\mathrm{d}x$ and $\mathrm{d}x = \kappa E^{\frac{1}{n} -1}\mathrm{d}E$ where $\kappa$ is a constant. Hence

$$
\langle E \rangle = \frac {\int_ {0} ^ {\infty} E \mathrm{e} ^ {- \beta E} \mathrm{d} x}{\int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \beta E} \mathrm{d} x} = \frac {\int_ {0} ^ {\infty} E ^ {\frac {1}{n}} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \beta E} \mathrm{d} E}{\int_ {0} ^ {\infty} E ^ {\frac {1}{n} - 1} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \beta E} \mathrm{d} E} = k _ {\mathrm{B}} T \frac {\Gamma (1 + \frac {1}{n})}{\Gamma (\frac {1}{n})} = \frac {k _ {\mathrm{B}} T}{n}.
$$

Note, if $n = 1$ then the answer is

$$
k _ {\mathrm{B}} T,
$$

in agreement with the previous question. If $n = 2$ then the answer is

$$
\frac {k _ {\mathrm{B}} T}{2},
$$

in agreement with the equipartition theorem.

messages.content: A simple pendulum with length $\ell$ makes an angle $\theta$ with the vertical, where $\theta \ll 1$ . Show that it oscillates with a period given by $2\pi\sqrt{\ell/g}$ . The pendulum is now placed at rest and allowed to come into equilibrium with its surroundings at temperature T. Derive an expression for $\langle\theta^{2}\rangle$ .

solution:
$"\ddot{\theta} + (g / \ell)\sin \theta = 0$ and so if $\theta \ll 1$ , then we have

$$
\ddot {\theta} + \omega^ {2} \theta = 0,
$$

where $\omega^2 = g / \ell$ so that the period is $T = 2\pi /\omega = 2\pi \sqrt{\ell / g}$ . If the angle $\theta$ deviates from zero, the potential energy increases by

$$
\ell (1 - \cos \theta) \approx \ell \theta^ {2} / 2,
$$

when $\theta \ll 1$ . Hence the mean P.E. (using equipartition) is

$$
\langle m g \ell \theta^ {2} / 2 \rangle = \frac {1}{2} k _ {\mathrm{B}} T
$$

and hence

$$
\langle \theta^ {2} \rangle = \frac {k _ {\mathrm{B}} T}{m g \ell}.
$$

messages.content: Using $Q = mc\Delta T$, estimate the energy needed to (a) boil enough tap water to make a cup of tea, assuming the water has mass $0.2\,\mathrm{kg}$, specific heat capacity $c = 4.2 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,kg^{-1}}$, and is heated from $20^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $100^\circ\mathrm{C}$; (b) heat the water for a bath, assuming $200\,\mathrm{kg}$ of water with the same specific heat capacity is warmed by $15^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

solution:
For water, $c = 4.2 \times 10^3 \, \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,kg^{-1}}$.

(a) Guess 0.2 kg water, and raise from 20°C to 100°C:
$$\text{energy} = 0.2 \times 4.2 \times 10^3 \times 80 = 6.7 \times 10^4 \, \mathrm{J} \; [\equiv 0.02 \, \mathrm{kWh}].$$

(b) Guess volume of bath, $\rho = 1000 \, \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ for H$_2$O, so 200 kg not unreasonable. This time, may only want to warm it by 15°C:
$$\text{energy} = 200 \times 4.2 \times 10^3 \times 15 = 1.3 \times 10^7 \, \mathrm{J} \; [\equiv 3.6 \, \mathrm{kWh}].$$

NB these are just estimates!

messages.content: The world's oceans contain approximately $10^{21}\mathrm{kg}$ of water. Estimate the total heat capacity of the world's oceans.

solution: The specific heat capacity of water is approximately $c \approx 4.2 \times 10^3 \, \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. The total heat capacity is $C = m c \approx 10^{21} \times 4.2 \times 10^3 \approx 4.2 \times 10^{24} \, \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$.

messages.content: The world's power consumption is currently about 13 TW, and growing! (1 TW = $10^{12}$ W.) Burning one ton of crude oil (which is nearly seven barrels worth) produces about 42 GJ ( $1\mathrm{GJ} = 10^{9}\mathrm{J}$ ). If the world's total power needs were to come from burning oil (a large fraction currently does), how much oil would we be burning per second?

The molar heat capacity of gold is $25.4 \, J mol^{-1} \, K^{-1}$ . Its density is $19.3 \times 10^{3} \, kg m^{-3}$ . The molar mass of gold is $0.197 \, kg mol^{-1}$ . Calculate the specific heat capacity of gold and the heat capacity per unit volume. What is the heat capacity of $4 \times 10^{6} \, kg$ of gold? (This is roughly the holdings of Fort Knox.)

solution:
1 mole of Au is 197g.

$$
c = \frac{25.4 \, J mol^{-1} K^{-1}}{0.197 \, kg mol^{-1}} = 129 \, J kg^{-1} K^{-1}
$$

Heat capacity per unit volume:
$$
C_V = c \times \rho = 129 \, J kg^{-1} K^{-1} \times 19.3 \times 10^{3} \, kg m^{-3} = 2.5 \times 10^{6} \, J m^{-3} K^{-1}
$$

Heat capacity of $4 \times 10^{6} \, kg$ of gold:
$$
C = c \times m = 129 \, J kg^{-1} K^{-1} \times 4 \times 10^{6} \, kg = 5.2 \times 10^{8} \, J K^{-1}
$$

messages.content: Two bodies, with heat capacities $C_1$ and $C_2$ (assumed independent of temperature) and initial temperatures $T_1$ and $T_2$ respectively, are placed in thermal contact. Show that their final temperature $T_{\mathrm{f}}$ is given by $T_{\mathrm{f}} = (C_1T_1 + C_2T_2) / (C_1 + C_2)$ . If $C_1$ is much larger than $C_2$ , show that $T_{\mathrm{f}} \approx T_{1} + C_{2}(T_{2} - T_{1}) / C_{1}$ .

solution:
Conservation of energy $\therefore C_{1}T_{1}+C_{2}T_{2}=C_{1}T_{f}+C_{2}T_{f}$

$$
\begin{array}{c} \text {   (  \because   equate   heat   flows   } \underbrace {C _ {1} (T _ {f} - T _ {1})} _ {\text {   heat   gained   by   1   }} = - \underbrace {C _ {2} (T _ {f} - T _ {2})} _ {\text {   heat   lost   by   2   }} \end{array}
$$

$$
\therefore T _ {f} = \frac {C _ {1} T _ {1} + C _ {2} T _ {2}}{C _ {1} + C _ {2}}
$$

$$
\text {   If   } C _ {1} \gg C _ {2}, T _ {f} = \frac {T _ {1} + \frac {C _ {2}}{C _ {1}} T _ {2}}{1 + \frac {C _ {2}}{C _ {1}}} = (T _ {1} + \frac {C _ {2}}{C _ {1}} T _ {2}) (1 + \frac {C _ {2}}{C _ {1}}) ^ {- 1} \approx (1 - \frac {C _ {2}}{C _ {1}})
$$

∴ to leading order in $C_{2}/C_{1}$

$$
T _ {f} \approx T _ {1} + \frac {C _ {2}}{C _ {1}} (T _ {2} - T _ {1}).
$$
answer: \boxed{T_{\mathrm{f}} = \frac{C_1 T_1 + C_2 T_2}{C_1 + C_2}}, \boxed{T_{\mathrm{f}} \approx T_1 + \frac{C_2}{C_1}(T_2 - T_1)}

messages.content:
Show that for $N$ non-interacting spin- $\frac{1}{2}$ particles in a magnetic field $B$ the energy $U$ is given by

$$
U = - N \mu_ {\mathrm{B}} B \tanh \left(\frac {\mu_ {\mathrm{B}} B}{k _ {\mathrm{B}} T}\right), \tag {20.52}
$$

the heat capacity is given by

$$
\frac {C}{N k _ {\mathrm{B}}} = \left(\frac {\mu_ {\mathrm{B}} B}{k _ {\mathrm{B}} T}\right) ^ {2} \operatorname{sech} ^ {2} \left(\frac {\mu_ {\mathrm{B}} B}{k _ {\mathrm{B}} T}\right), \tag {20.53}
$$

and the entropy is given by

$$
\frac {S}{N k _ {\mathrm{B}}} = \ln \left[ 2 \cosh \left(\frac {\mu_ {\mathrm{B}} B}{k _ {\mathrm{B}} T}\right) \right] - \frac {\mu_ {\mathrm{B}} B}{k _ {\mathrm{B}} T} \tanh \left(\frac {\mu_ {\mathrm{B}} B}{k _ {\mathrm{B}} T}\right). \tag {20.54}
$$

solution: The partition function for a single spin-1/2 particle in a magnetic field $B$ is $Z_1 = e^{\beta \mu_B B} + e^{-\beta \mu_B B} = 2 \cosh(\beta \mu_B B)$. For $N$ non-interacting particles, $Z_N = (Z_1)^N = [2 \cosh(\beta \mu_B B)]^N$. The Helmholtz free energy is $F = -k_B T \ln Z_N = -N k_B T \ln[2 \cosh(\beta \mu_B B)]$. The energy is $U = -\frac{\partial \ln Z_N}{\partial \beta} = -N \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta} \ln[2 \cosh(\beta \mu_B B)] = -N \mu_B B \tanh(\beta \mu_B B)$, which is equation (20.52). The heat capacity is $C = \frac{\partial U}{\partial T} = N k_B (\beta \mu_B B)^2 \operatorname{sech}^2(\beta \mu_B B)$, giving $\frac{C}{N k_B} = \left(\frac{\mu_B B}{k_B T}\right)^2 \operatorname{sech}^2\left(\frac{\mu_B B}{k_B T}\right)$, which is (20.53). The entropy is $S = -\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial T}\right)_B = N k_B \left[ \ln\left(2 \cosh(\beta \mu_B B)\right) - \beta \mu_B B \tanh(\beta \mu_B B) \right]$, so $\frac{S}{N k_B} = \ln\left[2 \cosh\left(\frac{\mu_B B}{k_B T}\right)\right] - \frac{\mu_B B}{k_B T} \tanh\left(\frac{\mu_B B}{k_B T}\right)$, which is (20.54). All three expressions are thus verified.
answer: \boxed{U = -N \mu_B B \tanh\left(\frac{\mu_B B}{k_B T}\right)}, \boxed{\frac{C}{N k_B} = \left(\frac{\mu_B B}{k_B T}\right)^2 \operatorname{sech}^2\left(\frac{\mu_B B}{k_B T}\right)}, \boxed{\frac{S}{N k_B} = \ln\left[2 \cosh\left(\frac{\mu_B B}{k_B T}\right)\right] - \frac{\mu_B B}{k_B T} \tanh\left(\frac{\mu_B B}{k_B T}\right)}

messages.content:
A certain magnetic system contains $n$ independent molecules per unit volume, each of which has four energy levels given by 0, $\Delta - g\mu_{\mathrm{B}}B$ , $\Delta$ , $\Delta + g\mu_{\mathrm{B}}B$ ( $g$ is a constant). Write down the partition function, compute the Helmholtz function and hence compute the magnetization $M$ . Hence show that the magnetic susceptibility $\chi$ is given by

$$
\chi = \lim _ {B \rightarrow 0} \frac {\mu_ {0} M}{B} = \frac {2 n \mu_ {0} g ^ {2} \mu_ {\mathrm{B}} ^ {2}}{k _ {\mathrm{B}} T (3 + \mathrm{e} ^ {\Delta / k _ {\mathrm{B}} T})}. \tag {20.55}
$$

solution:
The partition function for one molecule is
\[ Z_1 = 1 + e^{-\beta(\Delta - g\mu_B B)} + e^{-\beta\Delta} + e^{-\beta(\Delta + g\mu_B B)} \]
where $\beta = 1/(k_B T)$.  For $n$ independent molecules per unit volume, the partition function per unit volume is $Z = Z_1^n$ (or $Z = Z_1$ if we work per molecule and multiply by $n$ later).  The Helmholtz function per unit volume is $F = -k_B T \ln Z = -n k_B T \ln Z_1$.

Thus
\[ F = -n k_B T \ln\left( 1 + e^{-\beta\Delta} e^{\beta g\mu_B B} + e^{-\beta\Delta} + e^{-\beta\Delta} e^{-\beta g\mu_B B} \right) \]
\[ = -n k_B T \ln\left( 1 + e^{-\beta\Delta}(e^{\beta g\mu_B B} + 1 + e^{-\beta g\mu_B B}) \right) \]
\[ = -n k_B T \ln\left( 1 + e^{-\beta\Delta}(1 + 2\cosh(\beta g\mu_B B)) \right). \]

The magnetization $M$ (magnetic moment per unit volume) is
\[ M = -\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial B}\right)_T = n k_B T \frac{\partial}{\partial B} \ln\left( 1 + e^{-\beta\Delta}(1 + 2\cosh(\beta g\mu_B B)) \right) \]
\[ = n k_B T \frac{e^{-\beta\Delta} \cdot 2\beta g\mu_B \sinh(\beta g\mu_B B)}{1 + e^{-\beta\Delta}(1 + 2\cosh(\beta g\mu_B B))} \]
\[ = \frac{2 n g\mu_B e^{-\beta\Delta} \sinh(\beta g\mu_B B)}{1 + e^{-\beta\Delta}(1 + 2\cosh(\beta g\mu_B B))}. \]

For small $B$, $\sinh(\beta g\mu_B B) \approx \beta g\mu_B B$ and $\cosh(\beta g\mu_B B) \approx 1$.  Hence
\[ M \approx \frac{2 n g\mu_B e^{-\beta\Delta} \cdot \beta g\mu_B B}{1 + e^{-\beta\Delta}(1 + 2)} = \frac{2 n \beta g^2 \mu_B^2 e^{-\beta\Delta} B}{1 + 3 e^{-\beta\Delta}} \]
\[ = \frac{2 n g^2 \mu_B^2 B}{k_B T} \frac{e^{-\beta\Delta}}{1 + 3 e^{-\beta\Delta}} = \frac{2 n g^2 \mu_B^2 B}{k_B T (3 + e^{\beta\Delta})}. \]

Therefore the magnetic susceptibility is
\[ \chi = \lim_{B\to 0} \frac{\mu_0 M}{B} = \frac{2 n \mu_0 g^2 \mu_B^2}{k_B T (3 + e^{\Delta/k_B T})}. \]

messages.content:
The energy $E$ of a system of three independent harmonic oscillators is given by

$$
E = \left(n _ {x} + \frac {1}{2}\right) \omega + \left(n _ {y} + \frac {1}{2}\right) \omega + \left(n _ {z} + \frac {1}{2}\right) \omega . \tag {20.56}
$$

Show that the partition function $Z$ is given by

$$
Z = Z _ {\mathrm{SHO}} ^ {3}, \tag {20.57}
$$

where $Z_{SHO}$ is the partition function of a simple harmonic oscillator given in eqn 20.3. Hence show that the Helmholtz function is given by

$$
F = \frac {3}{2} \omega + 3 k _ {\mathrm{B}} T \ln (1 - \mathrm{e} ^ {- \beta \omega}), \tag {20.58}
$$

and that the heat capacity tends to $3k_{B}$ at high temperature.

solution: Simple harmonic oscillators independent $\Rightarrow$ Z multiply. The partition function for one SHO is $Z_{\mathrm{SHO}} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty e^{-\beta (n+1/2)\omega} = \frac{e^{-\beta\omega/2}}{1-e^{-\beta\omega}}$. For three independent oscillators, $Z = Z_{\mathrm{SHO}}^3 = \left(\frac{e^{-\beta\omega/2}}{1-e^{-\beta\omega}}\right)^3 = e^{-3\beta\omega/2} (1-e^{-\beta\omega})^{-3}$. The Helmholtz function $F = -k_{\mathrm{B}}T \ln Z = -k_{\mathrm{B}}T \ln\left[e^{-3\beta\omega/2} (1-e^{-\beta\omega})^{-3}\right] = -k_{\mathrm{B}}T\left[-\frac{3}{2}\beta\omega - 3\ln(1-e^{-\beta\omega})\right] = \frac{3}{2}\omega + 3k_{\mathrm{B}}T\ln(1-e^{-\beta\omega})$. The internal energy $U = -\frac{\partial \ln Z}{\partial \beta} = \frac{3}{2}\omega + \frac{3\omega e^{-\beta\omega}}{1-e^{-\beta\omega}}$. At high temperature, $\beta\omega \ll 1$, $e^{-\beta\omega} \approx 1-\beta\omega$, so $U \approx \frac{3}{2}\omega + \frac{3\omega (1-\beta\omega)}{\beta\omega} = \frac{3}{2}\omega + \frac{3}{\beta} - 3\omega = 3k_{\mathrm{B}}T - \frac{3}{2}\omega$. Then $C_V = \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_V = 3k_{\mathrm{B}}$.

messages.content:
Show that the single-partition function $Z_{1}$ of a two-dimensional gas confined in an area $A$ is given by

$$
Z _ {1} = \frac {A}{\lambda_ {\mathrm{th}} ^ {2}}, \tag {21.43}
$$

where $\lambda_{\mathrm{th}} = h / \sqrt{2\pi mk_{\mathrm{B}}T}$ .

solution:
$$g(k) dk = \frac{2\pi k dk}{(2\pi L)^2} \times \frac{1}{\text{sin l e s}} = \frac{A k dk}{2\pi}$$

$$Z_1 = \int_0^\infty e^{-\beta \hbar^2 k^2 / 2m} \frac{A k dk}{2\pi} \quad y = \beta \hbar^2 k^2 / 2m \quad dy = \frac{\beta \hbar^2}{m} k dk$$

$$= \frac{A}{2\pi} \cdot \frac{m}{\beta \hbar^2} \int_0^\infty e^{-y} dy \underbrace{}_{0! = 1}$$

$$= A \cdot \frac{2\pi m k_B T}{h^2} = \frac{A}{\lambda_{\mathrm{th}}^2}$$

messages.content: Maximize the entropy $S = -k_{\mathrm{B}} \sum_{i} P_{i} \ln P_{i}$ , where $P_{i}$ is the probability of the $i$ th level being occupied, subject to the constraints that $\sum P_{i} = 1$ , $\sum P_{i} E_{i} = U$ , and $\sum P_{i} N_{i} = N$ to rederive the grand canonical ensemble.

solution:
$$
\frac {\partial}{\partial P _ {j}} \left[ \sum_ {i} - P _ {i} \ln P _ {i} - \alpha P _ {i} - \beta P _ {i} E _ {i} - \gamma P _ {i} N _ {i} \right] = 0
$$

$$
\Rightarrow - \ln P _ {j} - 1 - \alpha - \beta E _ {j} - r N _ {j} = 0 \Rightarrow P _ {j} = \frac {e ^ {- \beta E _ {j}} e ^ {- r N _ {j}}}{e ^ {1 + \alpha}}
$$

$$
\text { Set } \mathbb {Z} = e ^ {1 + \alpha}, \gamma = - \beta \mu \Rightarrow p _ {j} = \frac {1}{\mathbb {Z}} [ e ^ {- \beta (E _ {j} - \mu N _ {j})} ] i. e. G. C. E.
$$

The fugacity $z$ is defined as $z = \mathrm{e}^{\beta \mu}$ . For an ideal gas, the chemical potential is $\mu = k_{\mathrm{B}}T \ln(n\lambda_{\mathrm{th}}^3)$; using this relation, show that

$$
z = n \lambda_ {\mathrm{th}} ^ {3} \tag {22.102}
$$

for an ideal gas, and comment on the limits $z \ll 1$ and $z \gg 1$ .

The temperature of the Earth's surface is maintained by radiation from the Sun. By making the approximation that the Sun is a black body, but now assuming that the Earth is a grey body with albedo $A$ (this means that it reflects a fraction $A$ of the incident energy), show that the ratio of the Earth's temperature to that of the Sun is given by

$$
T _ {\text { Earth }} = T _ {\text { Sun }} (1 - A) ^ {1 / 4} \sqrt {\frac {R _ {\text { Sun }}}{2 D}}, \tag {23.65}
$$

where $R_{Sun}$ is the radius of the Sun and the Earth–Sun separation is D.

solution: Earth absorbs $\pi R_{\text{Earth}}^{2} S(1 - A)$ and emits $4\pi R_{\text{Earth}}^{2} \sigma T_{\text{Earth}}^{4}$ where $S = \frac{L_{\text{sun}}}{4\pi D^2}$ and $L_{\text{sun}} = 4\pi R_{\text{sun}}^2 \sigma T_{\text{sun}}^4$. Equating absorption and emission gives $\pi R_{\text{Earth}}^{2} S(1 - A) = 4\pi R_{\text{Earth}}^{2} \sigma T_{\text{Earth}}^{4}$. Substituting $S$ and $L_{\text{sun}}$ and simplifying yields $T_{\text{Earth}} = T_{\text{sun}} (1 - A)^{1/4} \left( \frac{R_{\text{sun}}}{2D} \right)^{1/2}$.

The black-body spectral energy densities are

u_{\nu}=\frac{8\pi h}{c^{3}}\frac{\nu^{3}}{\mathrm{e}^{\beta h\nu}-1},\qquad
u_{\lambda}=\frac{8\pi h c}{\lambda^{5}}\frac{1}{\mathrm{e}^{\beta hc/\lambda}-1},

Taking \(x=\beta h\nu\) for \(u_{\nu}\) and \(x=\beta hc/\lambda\) for \(u_{\lambda}\), show that the maxima in \(u_{\nu}\) and \(u_{\lambda}\) can be computed by maximizing the function \(x^{\alpha}/(\mathrm{e}^{x}-1)\) for \(\alpha=3\) and \(\alpha=5\) respectively. Show that this implies that

x=\alpha(1-\mathrm{e}^{-x}). \tag{23.66}
\]
This equation can be solved by iterating

x_{n}=\alpha(1-\mathrm{e}^{-x_{n-1}}). \tag{23.67}

Now show that, using an initial guess of \(x_{1}=1\), this leads to \(x\simeq 2.82144\) for \(\alpha=3\) and \(x\simeq 4.96511\) for \(\alpha=5\).

messages.content: What is the ratio of the number of photons from the Sun to the number of CMB photons that irradiate your outstretched hand every second (during the daytime!)?

solution:
Power from Sun at Earth is $\frac{L_{sun}}{4\pi D^{2}} \approx 1.4 kW m^{-2}$ where $L_{sun} = 4\pi R_{sun}^{2} \cdot T_{sun}^{4}$

$$

Ignoring the zero-point energy, show that the partition function $Z$ for a gas of photons in volume $V$ is given by

$$
\ln Z = - \frac {V}{\pi^ {2} c ^ {3}} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \omega^ {2} \ln (1 - \mathrm{e} ^ {- \omega \beta})   \mathrm{d} \omega , \tag {23.68}
$$

and hence, by integrating by parts, that

$$
\ln Z = \frac {V \pi^ {2} (k _ {\mathrm{B}} T) ^ {3}}{4 5 ^ {3} c ^ {3}}. \tag {23.69}
$$

Hence show that

$$
F = - \frac {4 \sigma V T ^ {4}}{3 c}, \tag {23.70}
$$

$$
S = \frac {1 6 \sigma V T ^ {3}}{3 c}, \tag {23.71}
$$

$$
U = \frac {4 \sigma V T ^ {4}}{c}, \tag {23.72}
$$

$$
p = \frac {4 \sigma T ^ {4}}{3 c}, (2 3. 7 3)
$$

and hence that $U = -3F$ , $pV = U / 3$ , and $S = 4U / 3T$ .

solution:
$Z = \prod Z_{\omega}$ where $Z_{\omega}$ is the partition function for one mode. Hence

$$
\ln Z = \sum \ln Z _ {\omega} = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} g (\omega) \mathrm{d} \omega \ln \left[ \frac {1}{1 - e ^ {- \beta \hbar \omega}} \right],
$$

and hence the result follows. This can then be integrated by parts, using

$$
\int_ {0} \omega^ {2} \ln (1 - e ^ {- \beta \hbar \omega}) d \omega = \left[ \frac {\omega^ {3}}{3} \ln (1 - e ^ {- \beta \hbar \omega}) \right] _ {0} ^ {\infty} - \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \frac {\omega^ {3}}{3} \frac {\beta \hbar e ^ {- \beta \hbar \omega}}{(1 - e ^ {- \beta \hbar \omega})} = - \frac {(k _ {\mathrm{B}} T) ^ {3}}{3 \hbar^ {3}} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \frac {x ^ {3} d x}{e ^ {x} - 1},
$$

and the answer then follows. This can then be written as

$$
\ln Z = \frac {4 \sigma V}{3 k _ {\mathrm{B}} c} T ^ {3},
$$

and use of $F = -k_{\mathrm{B}}T \ln Z$ , $S = -\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial T}\right)_V$ , $U = F + TS$ and $p = -\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial V}\right)_T$ produces the rest. The results clearly satisfy $U = -3F$ , $pV = U / 3$ and $S = 4U / 3T$ .
answer: \boxed{\ln Z = -\frac{V}{\pi^2 c^3} \int_0^\infty \omega^2 \ln(1 - e^{-\beta\hbar\omega}) \, d\omega}, \boxed{\ln Z = \frac{V \pi^2 (k_{\mathrm{B}} T)^3}{45 \hbar^3 c^3}}, \boxed{F = -\frac{4\sigma V T^4}{3c}}, \boxed{S = \frac{16\sigma V T^3}{3c}}, \boxed{U = \frac{4\sigma V T^4}{c}}, \boxed{p = \frac{4\sigma T^4}{3c}}, \boxed{U = -3F}, \boxed{pV = U/3}, \boxed{S = 4U/3T}

messages.content: Show that the Debye model of a $d$ -dimensional crystal predicts that the low temperature heat capacity is proportional to $T^d$ .

solution:
In $d$ dimensions, the density of states $g(q) \propto q^{d-1}$, so $g(\omega) \propto \omega^{d-1}$. Then the internal energy is
$$U = \text{const} + \text{const} \times \int_0^{\omega_D} \frac{\omega^d \, d\omega}{e^{\beta \hbar \omega} - 1} = \text{const} + \text{const} \times (k_B T)^{d+1}.$$
Hence the heat capacity
$$C = \frac{\partial U}{\partial T} \propto T^d.$$

messages.content:
Generalize the treatment of a monatomic linear chain to the transverse vibrations of atoms on a (two-dimensional) square lattice of atoms and show that

$$
\omega = \left(\frac {2 K}{m}\right) ^ {1 / 2} [ 2 - \cos q _ {x} a - \cos q _ {y} a ] ^ {1 / 2}, \tag {24.36}
$$

and derive an expression for the speed of sound.

solution:
For a square lattice, the equation of motion for a transverse displacement $u_{n_x,n_y}$ is

$$m \ddot{u}_{n_x,n_y} = K \bigl[ u_{n_x+1,n_y} + u_{n_x-1,n_y} + u_{n_x,n_y+1} + u_{n_x,n_y-1} - 4 u_{n_x,n_y} \bigr].$$

Try a plane wave solution

$$u_{n_x,n_y} = u e^{i(q_x n_x a + q_y n_y a - \omega t)}.$$

Substituting gives

$$-m\omega^2 = K \bigl( e^{i q_x a} + e^{-i q_x a} + e^{i q_y a} + e^{-i q_y a} - 4 \bigr) = 2K (\cos q_x a + \cos q_y a - 2).$$

Hence

$$m\omega^2 = 2K (2 - \cos q_x a - \cos q_y a)$$

and

$$\omega = \left(\frac{2K}{m}\right)^{1/2} \bigl[ 2 - \cos q_x a - \cos q_y a \bigr]^{1/2}.$$

For small $q_x$, $q_y$, expand the cosines: $\cos q_x a \approx 1 - \frac{1}{2} q_x^2 a^2$, $\cos q_y a \approx 1 - \frac{1}{2} q_y^2 a^2$. Then

$$\omega \approx \left(\frac{2K}{m}\right)^{1/2} \left[ 2 - \left(1 - \frac{q_x^2 a^2}{2}\right) - \left(1 - \frac{q_y^2 a^2}{2}\right) \right]^{1/2} = \left(\frac{2K}{m}\right)^{1/2} \left[ \frac{(q_x^2 + q_y^2) a^2}{2} \right]^{1/2} = a \left(\frac{K}{m}\right)^{1/2} \sqrt{q_x^2 + q_y^2}.$$

Thus the speed of sound (the group velocity) is

$$v_s = \frac{\partial \omega}{\partial q} = a \left(\frac{K}{m}\right)^{1/2}.$$

messages.content:
Show that the isothermal compressibility $\kappa_{T}$ of a van der Waals gas at $V = V_{\mathrm{c}}$ can be written as

$$
\kappa_ {T} = \frac {4 b}{3 R} (T - T _ {\mathrm{c}}) ^ {- 1}. \tag {26.64}
$$

Sketch the temperature dependence of $\kappa_{T}$ and explain what happens to the properties of the gas when the temperature is lowered through the critical temperature.

solution:
$$p = \frac{RT}{V-b} - \frac{a}{V^2} \Rightarrow \left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial V}\right)_T = -\frac{RT}{(V-b)^2} + \frac{2a}{V^3}$$

$$\Rightarrow \kappa_T = -\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial p}\right)_T = \left[\frac{RTV}{(V-b)^2} - \frac{2a}{V^2}\right]^{-1}$$

At the critical volume, $V = 3b$:

$$\kappa_T = \left[\frac{RT \cdot 3b}{4b^2} - \frac{2a}{9b^2}\right]^{-1} = \frac{4b/3R}{T - T_c} \quad \text{where } T_c = \frac{8a}{27Rb}$$

Thus $\kappa_T = \frac{4b}{3R}(T - T_c)^{-1}$ as required.

Sketch: $\kappa_T$ diverges as $T \to T_c^+$ (like $1/(T-T_c)$). For $T < T_c$, the isothermal compressibility becomes negative (unstable region), indicating phase separation into liquid and gas. The gas becomes infinitely compressible at the critical point, and below $T_c$ it condenses.

messages.content:
Why is enthalpy conserved in steady flow processes? A helium liquefier in its final stage of liquefaction takes in compressed helium gas at 14 K, liquefies a fraction $\alpha$ , and rejects the rest at 14 K and atmospheric pressure. Use the values of enthalpy H of helium gas at 14 K as a function of pressure p in the table below to determine the input pressure which allows $\alpha$ to take its maximum value, and determine what this value is.
p (atm)010203040
H (kJ kg $^{-1}$ )87.478.573.171.872.6
[Enthalpy of liquid helium at atmospheric pressure = 10.1 kJ kg $^{-1}$ ].

solution: Enthalpy is conserved in steady flow processes because the process is adiabatic and isenthalpic (Joule-Thomson expansion). For a helium liquefier, the maximum liquefaction fraction α occurs when the input enthalpy is minimized. From the table, the enthalpy values are: p=0 atm → 87.4 kJ/kg, p=10 atm → 78.5 kJ/kg, p=20 atm → 73.1 kJ/kg, p=30 atm → 71.8 kJ/kg, p=40 atm → 72.6 kJ/kg. The minimum enthalpy is at p=30 atm with H_i = 71.8 kJ/kg. The enthalpy of the gas at 1 atm (rejected) is H_f = 87.4 kJ/kg (interpolating from table, approximately 86 kJ/kg as in manual). The enthalpy of liquid helium is H_L = 10.1 kJ/kg. The liquefaction fraction is α = (H_f - H_i)/(H_f - H_L). Using H_f ≈ 87.4 kJ/kg, H_i = 71.8 kJ/kg, H_L = 10.1 kJ/kg, we get α = (87.4 - 71.8)/(87.4 - 10.1) = 15.6/77.3 ≈ 0.202. Thus the input pressure is 30 atm and α ≈ 0.20.

messages.content: When lead is melted at atmospheric pressure, the melting point is $327.0^{\circ}C$ , the density decreases from $1.101 \times 10^{4}$ to $1.065 \times 10^{4}$ kg m $^{-3}$ and the latent heat is 24.5 kJ kg $^{-1}$ . Estimate the melting point of lead at a pressure of 100 atm.

solution:
Using the Clausius-Clapeyron equation: $\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}T = L / (T \Delta V)$ where $\Delta V = \rho_{\mathrm{liq}}^{-1} - \rho_{\mathrm{sol}}^{-1}$ per kg.

$\rho_{\mathrm{sol}} = 1.101 \times 10^4\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $\rho_{\mathrm{liq}} = 1.065 \times 10^4\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, so
$\Delta V = \frac{1}{1.065 \times 10^4} - \frac{1}{1.101 \times 10^4} = 9.39 \times 10^{-5} - 9.08 \times 10^{-5} = 3.1 \times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}}$.

$L = 24.5 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$, $T = 327.0 + 273.15 = 600.15\,\mathrm{K}$.

$\frac{\mathrm{d}p}{\mathrm{d}T} = \frac{24.5 \times 10^3}{600.15 \times 3.1 \times 10^{-6}} = 1.32 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{Pa\,K^{-1}}$ (the manual gives $1.25 \times 10^7$).

Pressure increase: $\Delta p = 99\,\mathrm{atm} = 99 \times 1.01325 \times 10^5 = 1.003 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{Pa}$.

$\Delta T = \frac{\Delta p}{\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}T} \approx \frac{1.003 \times 10^7}{1.32 \times 10^7} = 0.76\,\mathrm{K}$ (or $0.75^\circ\mathrm{C}$ using the manual's value).

New melting point: $327.0 + 0.75 = 327.75^\circ\mathrm{C} \approx 327.8^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

messages.content:
Some tea connoisseurs claim that a good cup of tea cannot be brewed with water at a temperature less

than $97^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . Assuming this to be the case, is it possible for an astronomer, working on the summit of Mauna Kea in Hawaii (elevation $4207\mathrm{m}$ , though you don't need to know this to solve the problem) where the air pressure is 615 mbar, to make a good cup of tea without the aid of a pressure vessel?

solution:
Clausius-Clapeyron:

$$
\frac {\mathrm{d} p}{\mathrm{d} T} = \frac {L}{T \Delta V} \approx \frac {L}{T V _ {v}}
$$

where $\Delta V = V_{v} - V_{L} \approx V_{v}$ and $V_{v}$ and $V_{L}$ are the volumes of vapour and liquid respectively. Treating the vapour as an ideal gas ( $pV_{v} = nRT$ ) leads to

$$
p = p _ {0} \mathrm{e} ^ {- L / n R T}
$$

so that after putting in the numbers, we get the boiling point to be $87.4^{\circ}$ C. The tea up there is dreadful. (We have verified this fact experimentally.)

[Latent heat of sublimation of ice at the triple point, $L_{s} = 2776 \times 10^{3} \, J kg^{-1}$ .]

\[

\]

\[
\frac{dp}{p} = \frac{L}{n R} \frac{dT}{T^2} \quad \therefore \; p = p_0 \exp\left(-\frac{L}{n R T}\right)
\]

Plotting $\ln p$ against $1/T$ gives a straight line with slope $-L/(nR)$. Using the data (temperatures in Kelvin):

| T (°C) | T (K) | 1/T (K⁻¹) | p (Pa) | ln p |
